script.opening: “Hi, doctor. Esi’s had diarrhoea and sickness — her mum told me to ring you. I’ve just come in from nights, so sorry if I’m a bit slow.”

facts.text: “Started Monday — so two days. Sick and the runs. The sick has stopped — last time was about four this morning. But the runs keep coming.”
“Six or seven nappies today already. Watery, yellowy. No blood, no slime.”
“Just milk and food. Not green, no blood. Three times yesterday.”
“She’ll only take little sips. Normally she guzzles her milk. She won’t eat.”
“Hmm… only two since last night. Normally she soaks five or six a day. The last one was about eight this morning.”

“She’s sleeping loads. When she’s awake she just lies on the sofa, whingey. Not playing with her toys. She did watch a bit of telly.” If asked to go and check her now: “She opened her eyes and looked at me, then cried a bit and went back to sleep.”

facts.topic: Other red flags (answer no if asked)
facts.text: No rash, no temperature today (38.1 yesterday), no fast or noisy breathing, no swollen tummy, no screaming with pain. Hands and feet feel warm. Lips “a bit dry”. If asked about tears: “I don’t know — she hasn’t really cried properly.”
“There’s a sickness bug going round her nursery. The twins are fine.”
Born on time, healthy, all jabs done, growing well. No medicines given except a bit of Calpol yesterday.

facts.topic: Practical situation (only if asked to bring her in or about getting to the surgery)
facts.text: “Why — is it serious?” Then: “I can’t today. My wife’s got the car at work till half seven, I’ve got the twins to pick up at quarter past three, and I can’t afford a taxi this week. Could I bring her tomorrow?”

facts.topic: Help available (only if the doctor asks whether anyone could help)
facts.text: “My brother-in-law, Kojo — he works from home, ten minutes away. He’s got a car. I could ask him.”
If offered a video call: “My phone screen’s smashed — the camera doesn’t work.”

You are tired, polite and keen not to make a fuss — you think it is “just a bug”. If the doctor offers tomorrow, accept with relief. If the doctor explains clearly why she needs to be seen today, you become worried and cooperative: “I didn’t realise. What should I do?” Mention Kojo only if asked about help. You also worry, if asked how you are, that you might nod off while watching her.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — practical: no car, no money for a taxi, twins to collect, and he is exhausted after a night shift and frightened he will fall asleep while watching her. He does not want to look like he is not coping, and his wife is more worried than he is.
ice.expectations: Advice on what to give her — “something to stop the runs”.

cues: “She’s just sleeping a lot.” — altered responsiveness, not ordinary tiredness.
“I’ve just come in from nights.” — an exhausted carer; practical barriers to come.
“Her mum told me to ring.” — another worried parent whose concern should be respected.

checkpoints.text: Takes a focused history: onset, frequency of diarrhoea and vomiting, blood, bilious vomit, fever, abdominal pain or swelling, rash, contacts
Assesses dehydration remotely and specifically: fluid intake, number of wet nappies, how responsive she is (asks father to check her now), dry lips, tears, colour, hands and feet

Recognises clinical dehydration with a red-flag feature (lethargy, reduced urine output) and that this needs face-to-face assessment today; considers alternative diagnoses (sepsis, intussusception, HUS) through red-flag questions

Arranges a face-to-face assessment within hours today and solves the transport barrier with the father (asks about family or friends, an afternoon slot, a duty-clinician home visit if no other option) — does not accept tomorrow

Gives interim oral rehydration advice: ORS in small frequent amounts (for example 5 mL every 1–2 minutes by spoon or syringe), stop juice and fizzy drinks, no anti-diarrhoeal medicines, keep a nappy count

Explicit 999 safety-net while waiting (hard to wake, mottled or cold hands and feet, very pale, fast breathing, no wet nappy, green vomit, blood in stool, non-blanching rash); hygiene and nursery exclusion until 48 hours after the last episode
Explains the reason for urgency without blame or alarm, respects the mother’s concern, and acknowledges his tiredness and constraints
Agrees a concrete, shared plan (who, how, when), checks understanding with teach-back, and confirms a call-back or appointment time

worked.txt: “When you say she’s sleeping a lot — could you go and look at her now while I hold on? Does she wake when you talk to her? Does she look at you?”
“How many wet nappies has she had since yesterday evening, compared with normal?”

“Most tummy bugs settle at home. But two things worry me: she’s weeing much less, and she’s more sleepy and floppy than normal. Those can be signs she’s getting dry. I need a doctor to see her today — not tomorrow.”
“I know you’ve no car and the twins to collect. Is there anyone — family, a neighbour — who could drive you this afternoon? I can hold a slot for you at two o’clock.”
“Get a rehydration drink like Dioralyte from the pharmacy. Give a teaspoon — 5 mL — every minute or two with a spoon or syringe. Little and often stays down better. No juice or fizzy drinks.”

“If she becomes hard to wake, goes very pale or blotchy, her hands go cold, she breathes fast, she has green sick or blood in her nappy, or a rash that doesn’t fade — call 999. Don’t wait for the appointment.”

f.learning: In children under 5 with gastroenteritis, the decision is not about the diagnosis but about dehydration and safety. NICE CG84 lists reduced urine output and altered responsiveness among symptoms of clinical dehydration, and altered responsiveness (lethargy or irritability) is a red-flag feature, so a child described as unusually sleepy with few wet nappies needs a face-to-face assessment the same day. Telephone assessment depends on converting vague words into data: count wet nappies, ask the parent to check the child while on the phone, and ask about colour, breathing, hands and feet and a rash. Red flags for other diagnoses include bilious vomiting, blood in the stool (HUS, intussusception), abdominal distension, high fever and a non-blanching rash. Interim management is oral rehydration solution little and often; avoid fruit juice and carbonated drinks; antidiarrhoeal drugs are not used in young children. The communication challenge is the parent who accepts a next-day appointment because of real barriers — the safe GP explains why, then helps solve the barrier (family, timing, a duty-clinician visit) rather than lowering the standard of care. Children should stay off nursery until 48 hours after the last episode (UKHSA).

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s: diagnosis and management (2009) · NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management (2019) · UKHSA — Health protection in children and young people settings, including education (2022)
knowledge.summary: Gastroenteritis with fewer wet nappies and new lethargy = clinical dehydration with a red flag: see today, solve the transport problem, ORS little and often, explicit 999 advice.

points.h: Who is at higher risk of dehydration
points.t: Under 1 year (especially under 6 months), low birth weight, six or more diarrhoeal stools or three or more vomits in 24 hours, not tolerating fluids, stopped breastfeeding, malnutrition.

Appears unwell or deteriorating; altered responsiveness (irritable, lethargic); decreased urine output; sunken eyes; dry mucous membranes; tachycardia; tachypnoea; reduced skin turgor. Red flags among these (unwell appearance, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnoea, reduced turgor) need particular attention.
Decreased level of consciousness, pale or mottled skin, cold extremities, very fast heart rate or breathing, weak pulses, prolonged capillary refill.

Bilious (green) vomiting or abdominal distension — obstruction; blood and mucus with colicky pain — intussusception; bloody diarrhoea with pallor or reduced urine — HUS; high fever, rash or neck stiffness — sepsis or meningitis; diabetic ketoacidosis in a child who is thirsty and drowsy.

No dehydration: continue usual fluids and food; supplement with ORS if at increased risk. Clinical dehydration: ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, given frequently in small amounts, with clinical monitoring — this is why the child must be assessed. For a 13 kg child that is about 650 mL over 4 hours. Avoid fruit juice and carbonated drinks.
Do not give antidiarrhoeal drugs (such as loperamide) to young children. Antibiotics are not routinely needed. Paracetamol or ibuprofen for distress or fever, with care if not drinking.
Hand washing with soap and water, no towel sharing, clean toilet and changing areas daily; exclude from nursery until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting.
The Clear pass candidate quantifies the nappies and responsiveness, explains the urgency in plain language, and works with the father to get Esi seen this afternoon.

model.text: Hello Mr Mensah, it’s Dr Hughes. Thanks for calling. Is Esi with you at the moment?
model.why: Confirms the caller and that the child is present

model.text: Yes, she’s on the sofa. She’s had diarrhoea and sickness for two days. I’ve just come in from nights.
Thank you — and well done for ringing after a night shift. Tell me what’s been happening.
The sick’s stopped, last at four. But the runs keep coming — six or seven today. And she’s just sleeping a lot.
Any blood in the poo, or green sick? Temperature, rash, or a swollen or very painful tummy?
No blood, not green. Temperature yesterday, not today. No rash.
How much is she drinking, and how many wet nappies since last night?
Just sips. Only two wet nappies — normally five or six.
Could you go and look at her now? Does she wake and look at you when you talk to her? What colour is she, and are her hands warm?
model.why: Real-time remote assessment of responsiveness and perfusion

model.text: She opened her eyes, cried a bit and went back to sleep. Hands are warm. Lips look a bit dry.

Thank you, that’s really helpful. I think this is a tummy bug from nursery. But she’s weeing much less and she’s more sleepy than normal, and in a little one those are signs she may be getting dry. I’d like a doctor to see her this afternoon.
model.why: Plain explanation of why face-to-face is needed today

model.text: Today? I can’t — my wife’s got the car till half seven, I’ve got the twins at quarter past three, and I can’t afford a taxi. Could I bring her tomorrow?
I understand — that’s a lot to juggle. I’m worried that waiting until tomorrow isn’t safe. Is there anyone — family, a friend, a neighbour — who could drive you here early this afternoon?
My brother-in-law, Kojo — he works from home and has a car.
Brilliant. I’ll book her in at half one, which gets you back for the twins. If Kojo can’t help, call me back straight away and we’ll arrange for a clinician to come to you.
Until then, pharmacy rehydration drink — Dioralyte — a teaspoon every minute or two. No juice or fizzy drinks, and no anti-diarrhoea medicine. Keep a note of wet nappies.

If she becomes hard to wake, goes very pale or blotchy, gets cold hands, breathes fast, has green sick, blood in her nappy or a rash that doesn’t fade — ring 999. And you’re very tired: is there someone who can sit with her if you need to sleep? Can you tell me the plan?
Ring Kojo, half one appointment, Dioralyte a spoon at a time, 999 if she’s floppy or pale or there’s blood. I’ll ask Kojo to stay.

social.t: Night-shift parents are sleep-deprived when daytime illness strikes. Ask who else can help, both for transport and supervision.
Transport costs are a real reason for missed or delayed care. Practices can hold a timed slot, a duty clinician can visit, and families often have help they will mention only if asked.

legal.t: A parent with parental responsibility can consent and give history; record who called and that the mother is aware.

professional.t: When remote assessment finds red-flag features, the duty is to arrange timely face-to-face assessment; document the features, the advice and the agreed time.
Make sure the afternoon clinician knows the concern; add a call-back task if the family do not attend.

community.t: ORS sachets are available without prescription; pharmacists can advise on preparation (one sachet in 200 mL of water).

redFlags: Bilious vomit, blood in stool, abdominal distension
Non-blanching rash, high fever, fast breathing, cold or mottled peripheries
psychosocial: Father after night shift, no car, cost
ice: Expectation: medicine to stop the diarrhoea

playbook.diagnosis: Acute viral gastroenteritis with symptoms of clinical dehydration and a red-flag feature (lethargy, reduced urine output) — needs face-to-face assessment today.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s most likely a tummy bug, but she’s weeing less and is more sleepy than usual, which can mean she’s getting dry. A doctor needs to see her today.”

management.reflectIce: “You were hoping for something to stop the runs, and getting here today is really hard. Medicines to stop diarrhoea aren’t safe for toddlers — the treatment is fluids — and she needs checking today, so let’s work out how.”
management.psychosocial: Use Kojo for transport and supervision; time the slot around the school run; offer a home visit as the back-up.
sharedPlan: If transport fails: call back — duty clinician home visit
ORS 5 mL every 1–2 minutes; no juice, fizzy drinks or antidiarrhoeals
Nappy count; hygiene; nursery exclusion until 48 hours symptom-free
safetyNet: 999: hard to wake, pale or mottled, cold hands and feet, fast breathing, green vomit, blood in stool, non-blanching rash, no wet nappy

pitfalls.intro: This feels like a routine “tummy bug” call. It is failed by candidates who accept vague words and the father’s offer of tomorrow.

items.fail: Accepts “she’s sleeping a lot” as normal tiredness and never counts wet nappies.
items.why: Lethargy and reduced urine output are the features that change management; without them the risk is invisible.
items.fix: Quantify: nappies since last night, and ask the parent to check her responsiveness while you wait.

items.fail: Agrees “bring her tomorrow” because the father cannot come today, with fluids advice.
items.why: A lethargic toddler with reduced urine output needs assessment within hours; deterioration can be quick.
items.fix: Hold the standard and solve the barrier: family transport, a timed slot, or a home visit; explicit 999 advice.

items.fail: Implies the father should have rung earlier or that he is not coping.
items.why: Blame makes parents less likely to call next time and does not get the child seen.
items.fix: Thank him, acknowledge the night shift, and plan together.

timeMap.d: Confirm caller and that the child is with him; acknowledge tiredness.
Frequency, blood, bile, fever, rash; intake; wet nappies; father checks responsiveness now.
Tummy bug, but signs of drying out — needs seeing today.
Who can drive? Timed slot; home visit as back-up; ORS amounts.
999 triggers, carer fatigue, nursery exclusion, teach-back.

wordPics.clearFail: Diagnoses a tummy bug, advises fluids and Calpol, and asks the father to call if worse — no nappy count, no responsiveness check, no face-to-face assessment.
wordPics.fail: Asks some dehydration questions and recognises concern but accepts tomorrow’s appointment, or tells the father to go to A&E without exploring how, and gives vague safety-netting.
wordPics.pass: Quantifies intake, nappies and responsiveness; recognises clinical dehydration; arranges a face-to-face assessment today with a workable transport plan; ORS advice; clear 999 triggers.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, done warmly: has the father check Esi in real time, explains urgency without blame, finds the brother-in-law, books a timed slot with a home-visit back-up, gives ORS in teaspoons, addresses his exhaustion, and closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Kids get sleepy when they’re ill — just keep pushing fluids.”
avoid.instead: “When you say sleepy — can you check whether she wakes and looks at you?”
avoid.why: Lethargy is a red flag, not a reassurance.

avoid.dont: “OK, bring her in tomorrow morning then.”
avoid.instead: “I’m worried waiting until tomorrow isn’t safe — who could help get you here this afternoon?”
avoid.why: The barrier is real but solvable; the risk is today.

avoid.dont: “Give her plenty of juice to keep her fluids up.”
avoid.instead: “Use a rehydration drink, a teaspoon every minute or two — not juice or fizzy drinks.”
avoid.why: Sugary drinks can worsen diarrhoea; ORS replaces salts.

ro.d: Follows “she’s just sleeping a lot”, “I’ve just come in from nights” and “her mum told me to ring”.
Idea (nursery bug); concern (cannot get there, exhausted); expectation (medicine to stop the diarrhoea).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — practical: no car, no money for a taxi, twins to collect, and he is exhausted after a night shift and frightened he will fall asleep while watching her. He does not want to look like he is not coping, and his wife is more worried than he is — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
